grade.first_issue: The claimed finiteness of P is false and is the first decisive defect. For a_1=2, the rule gives a_n=2n, so every prime q occurs in a_q=2q and P is infinite. The inference that a new prime p>M forces (a_n+M)/p<2 for large n is invalid. This false claim replaces the central argument, so Rule E caps the score at 3.
grade.summary: The submission makes useful preliminary observations about the global accepted set and bounded gaps, but its central finiteness argument concerns a set of primes that need not be finite. Consequently the asserted periodicity of C is not established. It also proves, at best, eventual periodicity and then unjustifiably extends it to every index. Establishing periodicity requires the new idea of passing to finitely many minimal accepted supports, rather than all prime factors occurring in the sequence.
strengths: Correctly translates the gcd conditions into intersections of prime supports.
Correctly proves a uniform gap bound using the radical of a_1.
Correctly observes that every sequence term belongs to the global accepted set C.
Recognizes that periodicity of C together with exact increasing enumeration would yield the desired translation law.

errors.description: The assertion that P=⋃S_n is finite is demonstrably false. With a_1=2, induction gives a_n=2n, yet P contains every prime. In particular, the claim that p>M implies (a_n+M)/p<2 for sufficiently large a_n has no valid basis and is false in this example.

Even after asserting only eventual enumeration and periodicity, the proof does not justify periodicity for all n. The statement that a_1 is the first element of C is literally false in general: for a_1=6 the sequence is 6,8,10,… while C contains 2. The appeal to determinism does not propagate an eventual relation backward, leaving the required universal range unhandled under Rule D.
